title: Facial Recognition & Biometric Privacy Security Checklist
metaDescription: Protect yourself from facial recognition surveillance and biometric data collection. Complete checklist to secure your biometric privacy rights.
intro: Facial recognition technology is everywhere - from retail stores to airports to social media platforms. This comprehensive checklist helps you protect your biometric privacy, opt out of facial recognition databases, and reduce your exposure to unwanted surveillance.

items.task: Use a privacy-focused browser like a privacy-focused browser
items.why: Prevents websites from using facial recognition on profile photos and blocks tracking scripts that could identify you through biometric data.
items.howTo: Use a privacy-focused browser or configure your current browser to block JavaScript on untrusted sites. Enable strict privacy settings and disable camera permissions for non-essential websites.

items.task: Disable facial recognition on all social media platforms
items.why: Social media companies use facial recognition to tag you in photos and build biometric profiles that can be shared with third parties.
items.howTo: On Facebook: Settings > Face Recognition > No. On Google Photos: Turn off face grouping. Review and disable similar features on Instagram, Twitter, and other platforms you use.

items.task: Remove metadata from photos before sharing online
items.why: Photo metadata can contain facial recognition data and location information that enables tracking and identification.
items.howTo: Use tools like ExifTool or online metadata removers before uploading photos. On smartphones, disable location services for camera apps and use apps that automatically strip metadata.

items.task: Regularly search for your photos online
items.why: Helps you discover if your images are being used without consent for facial recognition training or identification purposes.
items.howTo: Use Google Images, TinEye, and Yandex reverse image search monthly. Upload several photos of yourself to see where they appear online and request removal if found on unauthorized sites.

items.task: Review cloud photo storage facial recognition settings
items.why: Cloud services like iCloud and Google Photos automatically scan faces in your private photos to create biometric profiles.
items.howTo: In iCloud: Settings > Photos > People Album > Off. In Google Photos: Settings > Face grouping > Off. Consider using encrypted cloud storage alternatives like Tresorit or pCloud Crypto.

items.task: Opt out of Clearview AI database
items.why: Clearview AI has scraped billions of photos from the internet and sells access to law enforcement and private companies for facial recognition searches.
items.howTo: Visit Clearview AI's privacy page and submit an opt-out request with a government-issued ID. The process takes 2-3 weeks. Monitor for confirmation and follow up if needed.

items.task: Request removal from PimEyes face search engine
items.why: PimEyes allows anyone to upload a photo and find other images of the same person across the internet, posing significant privacy risks.
items.howTo: Contact PimEyes support to request removal of your images. Provide specific URLs where your photos appear in their results. This may require multiple requests and persistence.

items.task: Remove your photos from major data brokers
items.why: Data brokers collect and sell personal information including photos that can be used for facial recognition identification.
items.howTo: Submit removal requests to major brokers like Spokeo, BeenVerified, WhitePages, and Intelius. Use services like DeleteMe or manually submit requests following each broker's opt-out process.

items.task: Research and avoid stores using facial recognition
items.why: Many retailers use facial recognition for loss prevention, potentially creating databases of customer faces without explicit consent.
items.howTo: Check Fight for the Future's database of stores using facial recognition. Shop at privacy-conscious retailers when possible, or wear protective accessories in stores that use facial recognition.

items.task: Know your biometric privacy rights in your location
items.why: States like Illinois, Texas, and Washington have biometric privacy laws that give you legal recourse against unauthorized facial recognition use.
items.howTo: Research your local biometric privacy laws. In BIPA states, you can file complaints against companies that scan your face without consent. Keep records of unauthorized scanning incidents.

items.why: Many facial recognition systems use infrared light to map facial features, and IR-blocking accessories can interfere with this process.
items.howTo: Research glasses with IR-blocking coatings or infrared LEDs. Products like Reflectacles or DIY IR LED arrays can help disrupt facial recognition cameras in some situations.

items.why: Partial face coverings can significantly reduce facial recognition accuracy while remaining socially acceptable in many contexts.
items.howTo: Use masks, scarves, hats, or sunglasses strategically in high-surveillance areas. Vary your appearance patterns to make tracking more difficult. Understand local laws about face coverings.

items.task: Map facial recognition cameras in your regular locations
items.why: Knowing where facial recognition systems operate helps you make informed decisions about routes and protective measures.
items.howTo: Use apps like Surveillance Under Surveillance or research local camera installations. Note cameras at stores, transit systems, and public spaces you frequent. Plan alternative routes when needed.

items.task: Implement enhanced protection for activism and protests
items.why: Law enforcement and private contractors often use facial recognition at protests to identify and track activists, potentially leading to harassment or legal issues.
items.howTo: Use full face coverings, avoid bringing phones with face unlock, change your appearance significantly, and coordinate with others to use similar protective measures to maintain anonymity.

items.task: Understand facial recognition use in travel and transportation
items.why: Airports, border crossings, and transit systems extensively use facial recognition, often without opt-out options for travelers.
items.howTo: Research TSA facial recognition policies and opt-out procedures. Understand that border crossings may require compliance. Use ground transportation alternatives when possible for domestic travel.

pro_tips: Use different hairstyles, facial hair, or makeup patterns regularly to make facial recognition matching more difficult across time periods.
Enable two-factor authentication instead of face unlock on devices - biometric locks can be compelled by law enforcement in many jurisdictions.
Join local privacy advocacy groups to stay informed about new facial recognition deployments in your area and coordinate community responses.
Document instances of unauthorized facial recognition scanning with photos and timestamps - this evidence may be valuable for legal complaints under biometric privacy laws.
Consider the 'CV Dazzle' technique of using asymmetrical patterns in makeup or accessories specifically designed to confuse facial recognition algorithms.
